item.title: NVIDIA Advances Agentic Inference with Rubin Architecture and NVFP4 Numerical Precision
item.description:
NVIDIA Advances Agentic Inference with Rubin Architecture and NVFP4 Numerical Precision

NVIDIA is advancing its AI factory capabilities through the new Rubin architecture and NVFP4 precision. The company treats AI performance as a co-designed challenge involving GPU architecture, scale-up interconnects, serving software, CPUs, and storage to achieve significant throughput gains for agentic inference.

⚙️ Rubin Architecture and Performance

NVIDIA Rubin increases memory bandwidth significantly while maintaining capacity to optimize the most contested memory tier in AI factories.

  • Rubin memory bandwidth has risen to 19.2 TB/s, while capacity holds at 288 GB of HBM4.
  • The NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 delivers up to 30x the throughput per megawatt of the GB300 NVL72 at 160 tokens per second per user.
  • Each Rubin GPU provides 3.0 TB/s of NVLink 6 bandwidth, enabling approximately 20.7 TB of aggregate HBM4 across a rack.
  • Rubin adds inline memory tensor accelerator (TMA) descriptor updates, allowing one shared descriptor to serve experts with a common layout and reducing metadata overhead.

🧩 NVFP4 Numerical Precision

NVFP4 is a new numerical format that uses a 4-bit E2M1 element with two levels of scaling: an FP8 (E4M3) scale factor for every 16-value micro-block and a per-tensor FP32 scale. It has become the default precision for agentic benchmarks including AA-AgentPerf, SemiAnalysis AgentX, and MLPerf Endpoints.

Metric Benefit of NVFP4
Model Footprint 3.5x reduction relative to FP16; 1.8x reduction relative to FP8
KV Cache Footprint Up to 50% reduction compared to FP8
Resident Context Approximately 2x more context stays on device
Throughput Up to 4x the throughput of an FP8 baseline

🔍 Mixture-of-Experts Scaling

To manage Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models where all expert weights must reside in HBM, NVIDIA utilizes Wide expert parallelism (Wide-EP) through NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM.

  • Wide-EP: Spreads experts across eight or more GPUs. For DeepSeek-R1 at EP64, each GPU holds four experts per layer (232 blocks) instead of the full model.
  • Expert Parallel Load Balancer (EPLB): Redistributes hot and cold experts between forward passes to prevent GPU memory overcommitment.
  • NVLink Interconnect: On GB200 NVL72, 130 TB/s of aggregate NVLink bandwidth absorbs all-to-all dispatch and combine traffic.
  • Performance: Large EP (EP32) delivers up to 1.8x more output tokens per second per GPU than small EP (EP8) at 100 tokens per second per user.

💡 Distributed Serving with Dynamo

NVIDIA Dynamo acts as the distributed serving layer to manage the key-value (KV) cache, which stores intermediate attention calculations from previously processed tokens. The Dynamo router tracks where KV blocks reside and considers both worker load and cached-prefix overlap when placing requests. This architecture leads to higher cache-hit rates during prefill and less bandwidth consumption during decode.

Source: Five Ways NVIDIA Co-Design Maximizes the Value of Every Byte in the AI Factory | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: NVIDIA DSX MaxLPS Enables Higher GPU Density via Dynamic Power Sharing
item.description:
NVIDIA DSX MaxLPS Enables Higher GPU Density via Dynamic Power Sharing

NVIDIA and Nscale have evaluated DSX MaxLPS, a system that uses policy-governed power sharing to dynamically allocate power across resources, allowing customers to deploy up to 40% more GPUs within the same approved power budget.

💡 Why it matters

AI factories operate within a hierarchy of electrical limits, including utility service, substations, power-distribution equipment, racks, nodes, and GPUs. Traditional static power planning reserves enough power for every node to reach its specified peak simultaneously. However, AI workloads rarely draw constant power:

  • Training workloads: Move through compute, communication, synchronization, and checkpointing.
  • Inference workloads: Alternate between prefill, decode, memory-bound work, network activity, and idle intervals.
  • Variable requests: Even identical models draw different power based on concurrencies and request shapes.

Static reservations prevent unused capacity in one reservation from being applied to another node, leaving valuable infrastructure underused during normal operation.

🧩 How it works

DSX MaxLPS combines chip, system, thermal, and software technologies to maximize output within land, power, and shell (LPS) constraints. The Dynamic Power Software provides the control layer for the following process:

  • Infrastructure Mapping: Operators organize nodes into a managed group with an aggregate power budget.
  • Telemetry Collection: The system collects power telemetry from GPUs, nodes, racks, and groups at intervals sufficient to detect emerging power events and available headroom.
  • Policy Governance: Operator-defined rules establish group and node limits, allocation priorities, reserve requirements, and emergency or maintenance responses.
  • Dynamic Allocation: When some resources draw less than their allocation, the software adjusts GPU power limits so other resources can use that capacity, while maintaining the aggregate budget.

⚙️ Key details

A joint evaluation of this approach was conducted at Nscale’s data center at the Verne campus in Keflavík, Iceland, which is powered entirely by renewable energy. The technical walkthrough utilized the following configuration:

Component Detail
Systems NVIDIA GB300 NVL72
GPUs NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra
Workload Kimi K2.5 in FP4
Software NVIDIA Dynamo and NVIDIA TensorRT LLM
Sequence Length 8K input / 1K output
Workload Mix High-throughput and low-latency inference instances

#NVIDIA #DataCenter #GPU #EnergyEfficiency #AIInfrastructure

Source: How NVIDIA DSX MaxLPS Maximizes AI Factory Throughput and Efficiency | NVIDIA Technical Blog
